The predicted stability boundaries can be experimentally verified using STM or transport measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding correlated electron phases (Wigner crystals) in 2D materials like graphene, using advanced many-body techniques (HF/TDHF) to predict symmetry breaking and stability boundaries.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates Wigner crystallization (WC) in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, specifically determining if nematic phases (nWC) spontaneously break the threefold rotational symmetry ($C_3$) compared to standard $C_3$-invariant WC states.

**Main result.** Hartree-Fock calculations predict stable nWC regions favored over $C_3$-invariant WCs in certain parameter regimes due to kinetic energy gains, while TDHF analysis confirms stability for only half of the predicted nWC phases.

**Method.** The research employs projected Hartree-Fock (HF) and Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) calculations on a continuum model Hamiltonian. Stability is rigorously tested by analyzing the eigenvalues of the RPA stability matrix derived from TDHF.

**Model / system.** The system is rhombohedral tetralayer graphene ($	ext{R4G}$) modeled using a projected many-body Hamiltonian incorporating spin and valley degrees of freedom. Electron repulsion is treated via a screened Coulomb interaction.

**Key observables.** Nematicity diagnostic ($N$), stability eigenvalues from TDHF, anisotropic charge distribution (for STM), and direction-dependent depinning voltage (for transport measurements).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electron density ($n_e$) ranging from $0.2$ to $0.4 	imes 10^{12} 	ext{ cm}^{-2}$, and displacement fields ($V_{	ext{disp}}$) between $40$ and $100 	ext{ meV}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the projected HF framework, assuming a fixed two-body interaction; TDHF only proves local quadratic instability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 maps the HF phase diagram showing regions of $C_3$-symmetry violation (nWC) and instability. Figure 10 shows the smallest TDHF stability eigenvalue across the parameter space, distinguishing instabilities towards unit cell doubling (blue labels) versus metallic/stripe phases (red labels).

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first using HF calculations to identify symmetry-breaking nWC states in specific phase diagram regions. It then uses TDHF theory to test the local stability of these candidate WC states, identifying which ones are stable and predicting experimental signatures for their detection.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent experiments have reported evidence for Wigner crystals (WCs) in rhombohedral graphene. Here, we investigate Wigner crystallization in rhombohedral tetralayer graphene using projected Hartree-Fock (HF) calculations and time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) calculations. We first perform HF calculations with one electron per Wigner unit cell, and find nematic WCs (nWCs) that spontaneously break the threefold rotational symmetry $C_3$ and $C_3$-invariant WCs. In particular, there are two nWC regions in the phase diagram: one larger region at large displacement fields and low electron densities, and another smaller region at intermediate fields and high densities. Both the nWCs and the $C_3$-invariant WCs are valley-polarized states with zero Chern number, and have positive indirect gaps in the HF band structure. We then perform TDHF calculations to further test the local stability of the WC states. We find that all $C_3$-invariant WCs and half of the nWCs are locally stable, while the remaining nWCs are unstable towards WCs with two electrons per unit cell or metallic states. The predicted stable nWC phase can be identified experimentally by scanning tunneling microscopy through its anisotropic charge distribution or by angle-resolved transport measurements via a direction-dependent depinning voltage.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to engineer multiple quantum functionalities (spin, valley, magnetism) simultaneously through symmetry control using electric fields is highly relevant for designing next-generation quantum devices and strongly correlated electronic materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Investigating emergent electronic and magnetic phenomena, such as altermagnetism, Rashba splitting, and spin-valley locking, in inversion-asymmetric van der Waals heterostructures.

**Main result.** The $	ext{MnPS}_3|	ext{WS}_2$ heterostructure exhibits a rich interplay of these effects, forming a highly tunable platform whose electronic properties can be controlled by external electric fields and strain.

**Method.** First-principles calculations using Density Functional Theory (DFT) incorporating Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) and DFT-D2 corrections for van der Waals interactions.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a vdW heterostructure formed by stacking $	ext{MnPS}_3$ and $	ext{WS}_2$ monolayers. The study analyzes the electronic structure, magnetic ordering (altermagnetism), and spin-splitting effects at the interface.

**Key observables.** Electronic band gap ($\approx 1.65 	ext{ eV}$), type-I/type-II band alignment, Rashba spin splitting magnitude, valley polarization, and altermagnetic signatures.

**Important parameters / regimes.** External electric field (EEF) and in-plane biaxial strain are key tuning parameters; the system is analyzed near K and $ar{	ext{K}}$ valley points.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations rely on DFT approximations, which may underestimate band gaps and magnetic moments compared to experiments.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate unit cells, stacking configurations, electrostatic potential variations ($\Delta V$), spin-polarized band dispersions showing splitting at K/$ar{	ext{K}}$, and the evolution of band alignment under applied electric fields.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the crystal structure and methodology (DFT setup), presents results on emergent phenomena like altermagnetism, analyzes the tunability of band alignment via external fields, and concludes by establishing the material's potential for spintronics/valleytronics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The deliberate breaking of inversion ($\mathcal{P}$) symmetry in antiferromagnets has recently emerged as an effective means to induce various features, such as the emergence of Berry curvature, spin-valley locking, magnetoelectric coupling, and the transition from conventional antiferromagnetism to altermagnetism. Conversely, in non-magnetic systems, inversion symmetry breaking in the presence of strong spin-orbit interaction (SOI) gives rise to momentum-dependent spin splitting via the Rashba effect, enabling tunable spin polarization through external electric fields. Motivated by recent advances in two-dimensional materials, we perform first-principles calculations based on density functional theory to investigate the van der Waals (vdW) heterostructure formed by a $\mathcal{P}$-symmetric MnPS$_3$ monolayer and a WS$_2$ monolayer. We demonstrate that the interface hosts a rich interplay of emergent phenomena, including an altermagnetic phase, Rashba spin splitting, spin-valley locking, and valley polarization. Our results demonstrate that the heterostructure exhibits semiconducting behavior with a direct band gap of approximately 1.65~eV and a type-I band alignment. Remarkably, the electronic structure and band alignment can be effectively tuned between type-I and type-II regimes via an external electric field and in-plane biaxial strain. Furthermore, field-induced modulation enables strong control over the altermagnetic phase and the valley splitting. These findings establish the proposed vdW heterostructure as a highly tunable platform with significant potential for spintronic and valleytronic applications.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper derives a novel, general condition to test if nonseparable Werner states remain Bell local when subjected to multiple generalized measurement settings ($S_1 	imes S_2$). The authors show this new bound is stronger than previous known limits and provide explicit proofs showing that for sufficiently high dimensions relative to the number of measurements, all such states are necessarily local.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical bounds on quantum correlations, which is fundamental knowledge for understanding the limits of nonlocality in quantum information protocols that rely on entanglement testing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to find a new, general condition that determines when a nonseparable Werner state remains Bell local under arbitrary correlation scenarios involving $S_1 	imes S_2$ generalized quantum measurements.

**Main result.** A new general locality condition was derived for low-dimensional states ($d \le \min\{S_1, S_2\}$), which surpasses previous bounds. Furthermore, it is proven that high-dimensional nonseparable Werner states ($d > \min\{S_1, S_2\}$) are always $S_1 	imes S_2$-setting Bell local.

**Method.** The authors employ analytical techniques involving the construction and analysis of 'source operators' derived from the state. They establish an equivalence between Bell locality and admitting a specific type of Local Hidden Variable (LHV) description, which is then tested for tensor positivity.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on nonseparable Werner states ($	ext{W}_{d,\Phi}$) defined on a bipartite two-qudit system $\mathcal{H}_d \otimes \mathcal{H}_d$. The analysis extends to correlation scenarios involving $S_1$ and $S_2$ generalized measurements at each site.

**Key observables.** The degree of Bell nonlocality, quantified by the violation of various Bell inequalities under specific measurement settings ($S_1, S_2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** $S_1, S_2$ (number of measurement settings), $d$ (dimension of the Hilbert space), and $\Phi$ (the parameter characterizing the Werner state).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing an equivalence between Bell locality and the existence of a tensor positive source operator description for the correlations.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem by defining $S_1 	imes S_2$-setting Bell locality. It then derives the new general condition using source operators and establishes its equivalence to LHV models. Finally, it compares this new bound against established results (Werner's and Barrett's) and proves optimization results for specific dimension regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In many quantum applications it is important to know whether or not a Bell nonlocal two-qudit state exhibits its nonlocality under correlation scenarios with some given numbers $S_{1},S_{2}\geq1$ of generalized quantum measurements at two sites. In the present article, we find analytically a new general condition sufficient for a nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d\leq\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ to satisfy all Bell inequalities under every $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting correlation scenario with outcomes of an arbitrary spectral type, discrete or continuous $-$ that is, to be $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell local, for short. For a variety of $S_{1},S_{2}\geq1$ values, this new general locality condition is beyond Werner's and Barrett's locality conditions for a nonseparable Werner state. We also prove explicitly in the operator terms the optimization result by Terhal et. el. [Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{90,} 157903 (2003)] via semi-programming that every nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d>\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ is $S_{1}\times S_{2}$ -setting Bell local. The new results of the present article are important both for Bell nonlocality theory and for quantum applications based on Bell nonlocality.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper constructs a logical framework (QBism Logic) to formalize how agents update their beliefs based on quantum measurements. It achieves this by showing that the structure governing these updates can be translated into first-order logic over real closed fields, yielding a decidable calculus. Crucially, it demonstrates that standard finite-dimensional quantum mechanics fits perfectly within this abstract mathematical structure.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep mathematical foundation connecting operational quantum theory to formal logic and model theory. For theorists working on open quantum systems or measurement processes, it offers a rigorous, decidable calculus for reasoning about state updates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a rigorous logical formalization of QBism (Quantum Bayesianism), interpreting quantum theory as a normative framework for an agent's probability assignments and their revision based on experience.

**Main result.** It establishes that the structure describing quantum updates, when restricted to effectively semialgebraic data over real closed fields, yields a sound, complete, and decidable recursive calculus. Furthermore, it shows standard finite-dimensional QM fits this framework using SIC coordinates.

**Method.** The methodology involves developing a guarded dynamic language for histories, translating the logic fragment into first-order formulas in ordered rings, and applying algebraic geometry tools (qplex conditions) to verify quantum realizations.

**Model / system.** The model is QBism Logic applied to finite-dimensional quantum systems. The core structure is defined by a 'well-formed core datum' $(Q, \mathcal{D}, B, U)$, involving admissible prior spaces, measurement families ($\mathcal{D}$), Born kernels ($B$), and update kernels ($U$).

**Key observables.** Posterior reference priors ($	ext{up}_\pi(h)$) and history probabilities ($r_\pi(h)$). Diagnostics include consistency bounds and the lower polar condition.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension parameter $d \ge 2$, and the underlying structure is assumed to be effectively semialgebraic over a real closed field $K$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumes the existence of an SIC reference measurement in finite dimensions, and relies on explicit coefficient field hypotheses for the effective semialgebraic reduction theorem.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining the general logical structure (Chunk 2), then proving a global reduction theorem to eliminate dynamic operators (Chunk 1/4), followed by translating this into first-order logic over real closed fields for decidability (Chunk 1/4), and finally demonstrating that standard quantum mechanics realizes this framework under SIC assumptions, confirming its semialgebraic nature (Chunk 3).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

QBism interprets quantum theory as a normative discipline for an agent's probability assignments and their revision across possible experience. This paper develops a logical formalization of that picture. A well-formed core datum consists of an admissible prior space, a finite family of actual measurements, Born kernels, and update kernels. For each such datum, we introduce a guarded dynamic language for histories and posterior states and prove a global reduction theorem. We next consider effectively semialgebraic data over an effectively presented real closed field. For data in this class, we translate the fragment without dynamic operators into first-order formulas in the corresponding language of ordered rings, thereby reducing validity to first-order reasoning over real closed fields. Together, the reduction and first-order translation yield a sound and complete recursive calculus and a decision procedure for validity. Finally, assuming a symmetric informationally complete (SIC) reference measurement, we show that quantum theory in finite dimensions realizes the framework through SIC coordinates, POVMs, and quantum instruments. We also prove that the corresponding SIC image satisfies the standard qplex geometry conditions, namely the consistency bounds and the lower polar condition, and that under explicit coefficient field hypotheses the resulting quantum datum is effectively semialgebraic.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the fundamental question of how many physical degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle system compared to classical expectations. It demonstrates that in quantum mechanics, constraints fail to eliminate all variables as they do classically, leading to generalized uncertainty relations defining the Quantum Reference Frame. The work critically assesses modern relational models by showing their potential inconsistencies with established symmetries like Galilean invariance.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly focused on AMO systems, its deep dive into foundational quantum mechanics, constraints, and reference frames is crucial background knowledge for any advanced theorist working on open quantum systems or quantum gravity where defining a 'physical' observable relative to an observer/frame is paramount.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental discrepancy between classical and quantum descriptions regarding the number of physical degrees of freedom for an N-particle system, particularly concerning constraints imposed by conservation laws.

**Main result.** Unlike classical physics where constraints eliminate unphysical center-of-mass variables, in quantum mechanics all canonical degrees of freedom are considered physical, leading to generalized uncertainty relations (GURs) that define the Quantum Reference Frame (QRF).

**Method.** The authors employ theoretical analysis, contrasting Lagrangian/Hamiltonian formalisms from classical mechanics with advanced quantization procedures and symmetry considerations in quantum theory.

**Model / system.** The system under study is a general N-particle quantum mechanical state. The formalism compares canonical descriptions to those derived from relational models (QRFs) that attempt to eliminate background spacetime dependence.

**Key observables.** Degrees of freedom, Generalized Uncertainty Relations (GURs), and the structure of the Quantum Reference Frame (QRF).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of particles N; constraints derived from momentum conservation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** It assumes that a canonical description is possible but critically challenges the assumption in some relational models that all physical dynamics must be purely relational or derivable solely from symmetries like Galilean invariance.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the classical vs. quantum discrepancy regarding degrees of freedom, then critiques existing 'relational QRF models' by testing their consistency with fundamental symmetries (like Galilean invariance), and finally applies canonical theory to derive GURs for the QRF.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational. Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed

</details>

**Summary.** This work provides a rigorous derivation of Richards' equation from a mesoscopic kinetic theory describing water flow in soil. It uses the Chapman-Enskog expansion to bridge the gap between microscopic pore dynamics and macroscopic continuum laws. Furthermore, it applies spectral analysis to derive advanced permeability models for structured media directly from connectivity properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on porous media flow, the mathematical machinery—using spectral analysis (eigenvectors/eigenvalues) to decompose a complex operator into simpler, interacting subsystems (two bands)—is highly analogous to techniques used in quantum many-body physics for modeling coupled quantum systems or domain decomposition in QEC.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper derives Richards' equation for unsaturated soil water flow by rigorously separating two limits—spatial and temporal—that are often conflated in standard macroscopic theories.

**Main result.** It successfully derives the continuum balance (Richards' equation) from a mesoscopic kinetic description by applying a Chapman-Enskog reduction, providing first-principles derivations for permeability models like dual-permeability.

**Method.** The core methodology involves performing a Chapman-Enskog expansion on a Continuum Kinetic Equation (CKE), which itself is obtained via a gradient expansion (spatial limit) of the pore-filling distribution dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system models unsaturated soil water flow, governed by the evolution of the pore-filling distribution $g(r, x, t)$ within Representative Elementary Volumes (REVs). The analysis extends to bimodal distributions, allowing for spectral decomposition and domain reduction techniques.

**Key observables.** Hydraulic Conductivity ($K$), Water Content ($	heta$), Retention Curve, Inter-domain Exchange Coefficient ($\Gamma_w$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Damköhler Number (Da), which controls the temporal separation; pore size distribution characteristics (e.g., bimodal gap).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions are that the system can be reduced via a small Damköhler number expansion ($Da \ll 1$) and, in advanced sections, that spectral gaps exist to justify domain decomposition.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the derivation path from CKE $	o$ Richards' equation; spectral analysis shows eigenvalue gaps ($\lambda_1$) confirming the validity of two-domain reductions by showing rate ratios approaching unity as separation increases.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a multi-stage reduction: first, establishing the CKE via spatial limit; second, applying CE expansion in time to yield Richards' equation and identifying $K$; finally, using spectral theory on bimodal systems to derive inter-domain exchange coefficients from first principles.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Richards' equation for unsaturated water flow is derived from the kinetic theory of the pore-filling distribution g(r,x,t) of a companion paper. It separates two limits that macroscopic theory usually conflates. The spatial limit is purely kinematic: contracting the representative elementary volume (REV) to a point yields the closed continuum kinetic equation (CKE) d_t g + div F = C[g], with F a pore-resolved pre-closure flux and C[g] the occupancy-gated redistribution operator. The dynamics lies in the temporal limit, the subject of this paper: a Chapman-Enskog (CE) reduction of the CKE controlled by the Damkohler number Da (redistribution time over forcing time), the structural analogue of the passage from Boltzmann to Navier-Stokes. The linearized redistribution operator J is self-adjoint and negative semidefinite in the mass inner product, with a one-dimensional kernel fixing a single invariant (water) and hence one macroscopic equation; the CE hierarchy inverts the same J at every order, only the source changing. Four results follow: the equilibrium step defines the retention curve; the linearized water budget plus the inter-REV source set the first-order equation; its solvability is mass conservation, i.e. Richards' equation; and the response function gives the macroscopic flux, identifying the conductivity K as a first-order transport coefficient, the counterpart of viscosity. Mean-field reduction recovers the standard integral formula; the serial-path correction gives Mualem's heterogeneity penalty. A bimodal pore-size distribution opens a gap in the relaxation spectrum; projecting onto the bands and applying CE within each, with cross-band relaxation surviving at O(1), derives the dual- and multiple-permeability models from first principles, the exchange coefficient set by inter-band connectivity. When Da is not small the expansion breaks down and the full CKE is needed.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes the mathematical properties—specifically the Hausdorff dimension and survival tail—of computational histories that run forever despite being almost surely terminating. It achieves this by developing powerful bounds on source-power sums using matrix theory, demonstrating how subtle differences in local rules can lead to vastly different global nontermination behaviors.

**Why it may be interesting.** While highly abstract, the rigorous mathematical framework developed for bounding complexity and dimension in infinite random processes has parallels with analyzing long-time behavior or rare events in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper studies the survival tail, Kolmogorov complexity, and Hausdorff dimension of exceptional random tapes for randomized algorithms that are guaranteed to terminate almost surely.

**Main result.** It establishes bounds on source-power sums ($Z_{\Lambda}^T(s)$) using matrix commutation properties, showing that nontermination dimensions can differ drastically even when ordinary kernels match.

**Method.** The analysis employs advanced tools from information theory and probability, including Rényi entropy sums, powered action matrices, and dimension calculations derived from source-power bounds.

**Model / system.** The model is a randomized computation process defined by a source law $P$ on the tape $\omega$, focusing on the set of tapes where the repair process never stops ($	au(\omega) = \infty$).

**Key observables.** Survival tail ($P\{	au \geq T\}$), Source-power sum ($Z_{\Lambda}^T(s)$), Effective dimension ($	ext{Dimeff},_P(\omega)$), and Hausdorff dimension.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The exponent $s$ (where $s=1$ controls termination) and structural parameters related to the underlying computation graph or source law are critical.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis requires specific structural conditions, such as powered action matrices commuting for certain values of $s$, and relies on definitions involving 'source-power domination'.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes; the focus is on mathematical theorems and derived bounds.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops results by first defining the survival tail and source-power sums, then using matrix commutation properties (Theorem 2.3) to bound these sums for various $s$. It applies these general tools to specific problems like k-SAT and provides exact likelihood ratio identities for finite runs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A randomized algorithm may terminate almost surely even though exceptional random tapes make it run forever. This paper studies the survival tail, the Kolmogorov complexity of one such tape, and the Hausdorff dimension of all of them. For each $s>0$ at which the powered repair matrices commute, the main theorem bounds $\sum_wP[w]^s$ over surviving prefixes $w$, uniformly over deterministic nonanticipating selectors. The case $s=1$ controls termination; the full family gives weak-source and dimension bounds.   The source powers contain information absent even from the ordinary repair kernel and the complete stopping-time law. Under one common finite tape source, two overlapping disagreement-repair rules on a four-vertex path have the same ordinary kernels and the same stopping-time law for every selector, yet their nontermination dimensions can be arbitrarily close to zero and one. At one common source-power level, the same dominated tape source makes one rule run forever but gives the other an exponential stopping tail. The separation is caused by action labels that produce the same state transition and are therefore invisible at power one. For bounded-dependence $k$-SAT, conditional block min-entropy above the trace-growth threshold gives exponential termination, and the effective dimension of an individual infinite run is bounded by the trace growth induced by the clauses repaired infinitely often. Tree formulas asymptotically attain the maximum-degree dimension and global source bounds, while clique formulas attain the graph-specific one-step threshold in the stated regime. An exact backward likelihood identity complements these setwise results with tail and coding bounds for each run.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper develops a theoretical framework to detect the Unruh effect by measuring acceleration-dependent effects on an atom. It optimizes measurement parameters—including probe time and initial state—to minimize the uncertainty in estimating the acceleration factor. The results show that careful optimization can significantly reduce the required experimental time, suggesting feasibility with advanced atomic systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed roadmap for experimental verification of fundamental QFT predictions (Unruh effect) using controllable quantum systems like trapped atoms, combining advanced concepts from open quantum systems and metrology.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the quantum metrological detection of the Unruh effect, which involves verifying acceleration-dependent modifications predicted by quantum field theory for uniformly accelerated observers.

**Main result.** The minimal uncertainty in estimating the acceleration factor can be significantly reduced by optimizing the individual probe interaction time and utilizing atoms with larger transition dipole moments. The optimal initial state depends critically on whether the acceleration is small or large.

**Method.** Quantum metrology principles are applied to bound the estimation uncertainty using the Fisher information, requiring optimization over the probe evolution time, initial atomic state, and measurement basis.

**Model / system.** The system involves a two-level probe atom coupled to the vacuum electromagnetic field while undergoing uniform acceleration. The dynamics are modeled using an effective Hamiltonian derived from the multipolar coupling scheme.

**Key observables.** Minimal estimation uncertainty ($	ext{Var}(X)$) of the acceleration factor ($X = a/(c\omega_0)$), and the Fisher information ($F_X$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Acceleration factor $X$, individual probe evolution time $	au$, total probe time $T$, initial atomic state parameters ($\cos	heta, \sin	heta$), and transition dipole moments.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the electromagnetic field is initially in a vacuum state (inertial observer frame) and utilizes weak coupling approximations for the density matrix evolution.

**Figures summary.** Figures 1-3 show optimized quantities ($F_X/\epsilon_	au$) versus $\epsilon_	au^{-1}$ for various initial states at fixed accelerations. Figure 4 shows this ratio dependence on $X$ for fixed probe times, illustrating optimal parameter choices.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using quantum metrology bounds and then systematically optimizes the estimation uncertainty by varying the individual probe time ($	au$), initial state, and measurement basis across different acceleration regimes ($X=0.8, 5, 20$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

For a uniformly accelerated two-level probe atom, the acceleration-dependent factor is encoded in the atomic state during the atom-field evolution. If this factor can be estimated through a large number of measurements with an uncertainty smaller than its magnitude, the Unruh effect can be experimentally verified. In this work, we show that the minimal uncertainty is inversely proportional to the square root of the total probe time. For a fixed total probe time, we minimize the estimation uncertainty by optimizing the atom-field interaction time, the initial atomic state, and the measurement basis in each probe. Results show that the uncertainty decreases as the evolution time of each individual probe becomes shorter. The optimal measurement basis is determined by the initial atomic state, while the optimal initial state depends on both the acceleration factor and the evolution time of each probe. For a fixed evolution time, we analyze the estimation uncertainty versus the acceleration factor and identify the optimal factor and minimal uncertainty for each initial state. The initial excited state outperforms other configurations in the small-acceleration regime, whereas the ground state can become advantageous for sufficiently large acceleration and long evolution time of each probe. Finally, we estimate the minimal total probe time required for testing the Unruh effect and demonstrate that it can be significantly reduced by using probe atoms with larger transition dipole moments.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes a three-body Hopfield model on sparse random graphs using advanced replica methods. It finds that three-body interactions fundamentally alter the memory retrieval process, causing discontinuous transitions and robust glassy trapping behavior. The work clarifies how both many-body complexity and graph sparsity govern the system's storage capacity.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical neural networks, the analysis of phase transitions, glassy dynamics, and mean-field approximations in disordered systems provides methodological parallels to understanding complex quantum many-body ground states or optimization problems in quantum computing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the statistical mechanics of a three-body Hopfield model defined on sparse random graphs with finite mean connectivity.

**Main result.** Three-body interactions induce a discontinuous retrieval transition, leading to a spin-glass-like trapping mechanism at low temperatures that is distinct from conventional two-body models.

**Method.** The analysis employs the replica-symmetric (RS) functional framework combined with Population Dynamics (PD) for self-consistent equation solving, complemented by finite-size Monte Carlo simulations.

**Model / system.** The model is a three-body Hopfield network described by a Hamiltonian involving three-spin couplings ($J_{ijk}$) on sparse random graphs. The system's behavior is characterized by the interplay between many-body interactions and graph disorder.

**Key observables.** Local-field distribution $W_\xi(h)$, retrieval order parameter, spin-glass overlap $q$, and characteristic storage load $\alpha$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mean connectivity ($c=O(1)$), number of patterns ($P$), normalized load ($\alpha = P/c$), and temperature/inverse temperature ($eta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary analytical tool relies on the Replica Symmetric (RS) ansatz, which is acknowledged to break down in the low-temperature glassy regime.

**Figures summary.** Figure 6 illustrates the mean-connectivity dependence of critical load parameters ($\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$), showing that storage capacity scales linearly with connectivity ($P \propto c$).

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure: model introduction, free energy evaluation via replica method using functional integrals, solving self-consistent equations via Population Dynamics (PD), comparison with Monte Carlo simulations, and final discussion on the implications of many-body effects.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A three-body Hopfield model defined on sparse random graphs with finite mean connectivity is studied using a replica-symmetric (RS) analysis. By extending the functional replica framework for conventional two-body finite-connectivity Hopfield models, self-consistent equations for the local-field distribution are derived and solved numerically by population dynamics. In contrast to two-body sparse Hopfield models, three-body interactions induce a discontinuous retrieval transition, coexistence of paramagnetic and retrieval solutions, and a distinct spinodal structure. Starting the RS population dynamics from an uninformative finite-amplitude field distribution leads to a spin-glass-like fixed point at low temperatures rather than to the retrieval state. This trapping already occurs for a single embedded pattern, where conventional cross-talk noise among stored patterns is absent, indicating that it originates from the combination of sparse connectivity and three-body interactions. Within the RS description, increasing the number of embedded patterns drives a crossing between the retrieval and glassy free-energy branches, making the glassy branch thermodynamically stable at high load. Finite-size Monte Carlo simulations using population annealing support the RS description of the retrieval branch and reproduce the trapping behavior under cooling, while deviations from the RS spin-glass branch point to replica-symmetry breaking in the low-temperature glassy regime. The characteristic storage load scales linearly with the mean connectivity, reflecting the sparse number of couplings. These results clarify how many-body discontinuity and sparse graph disorder simultaneously influence the accessibility and capacity of associative memory.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a statistical approach to model adverse selection, treating market quality deterioration as a dynamic truncation of the underlying quality distribution. It determines critical conditions based on buyer payment rates and initial quality variance required to prevent the market from collapsing entirely. The findings offer insights into how interventions can stabilize imperfect markets.

**Why it may be interesting.** While applied to economics, the mathematical framework of sequential conditional distribution updates and stability analysis under constraints (truncation) shares formal parallels with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models involving filtering or boundary effects in quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes adverse selection in markets driven by asymmetric information, which causes market deterioration by eliminating high-quality goods.

**Main result.** It establishes conditions (related to the payment rate $\xi$ and minimum quality floor $q_0$) necessary to prevent complete market collapse, showing that variance and price premium jointly determine the speed of deterioration.

**Method.** The analysis models the process as a dynamic truncation of the underlying quality distribution, using recursion relations derived from conditional probability distributions.

**Model / system.** The system is an economic model where buyers set an upper bound ($b_t = \xi ar{q}_t$) on payment, causing sellers with quality $q > b_t$ to exit. The market state evolves by retaining the conditional distribution of quality.

**Key observables.** Mean market quality ($ar{q}_t$), retained-market variance ($\sigma^2_{t+1}$), and the price premium ($a_t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The payment rate $\xi$, the underlying quality variance parameter ($s^2$), and the minimum quality floor ($q_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The market deterioration path is assumed to be monotone ($ar{q}_{t+1} < ar{q}_t$); the analysis uses maximum-entropy principles for benchmark distributions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate mean-quality dynamics showing convergence to a stable platform when $\xi > \xi_c$, and demonstrate market collapse versus avoidance based on whether a positive floor exists (comparing $\xi < 2$ vs. $\xi > 2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first defines the dynamic truncation process, derives bounds on mean quality decline using variance and price premium, then uses maximum-entropy methods to find benchmark distributions, and finally discusses implications for market interventions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The adverse-selection mechanism in markets explains how asymmetric information between buyers and sellers can drive high-quality goods out of the market, thereby causing market deterioration. In its simplest formulation, only the mean quality is used to describe the market, and this is insufficient to determine how fast the market deteriorates or how the quality distribution evolves. To resolve the two problems, we describe the adverse selection as a dynamic truncation of the quality distribution: buyers set an upper bound proportional to the mean quality by a rate $ξ$ that is larger than unity, and sellers whose quality exceeds this upper bound reject an offer and exit the market. The retained market is then characterized by the conditional distribution obtained after this truncation, and the corresponding evolution process is iterated until market quality reaches a stable state. This statistical approach gives three results. (i) We identify a mechanism for preventing complete adverse selection, defined as the process where the quality of the market is driven down to the minimum quality floor. (ii) A larger quality variance or a smaller price premium, defined as the amount by which the payment upper bound exceeds the current mean quality, raises the upper bound on the deterioration in mean quality. (iii) A maximum-entropy benchmark shows numerically how quality variance and the payment rate jointly determine market deterioration and the final stable quality platform. This approach also clarifies how market interventions can slow adverse selection: they may raise buyers' payment rate, reduce quality variance, or increase the minimum quality floor.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a novel multilevel quantum algorithm to estimate observables derived from parabolic Partial Differential Equations. It successfully overcomes the major bottleneck of classical and direct quantum methods: the polynomial dependence on the fine spatial mesh size ($h^{-1}$). By coherently encoding fine-to-coarse level differences, it achieves an exponential reduction in complexity with respect to $h^{-1}$.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses simulating time evolution governed by PDEs (like heat diffusion) on quantum hardware, which is crucial for modeling open quantum systems or thermalization processes in condensed matter theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a quantum algorithm that estimates observables related to Parabolic PDEs without incurring a computational cost polynomial in the inverse of the spatial mesh size ($h^{-1}$).

**Main result.** A multilevel quantum algorithm is developed that achieves an end-to-end complexity independent of the finest mesh size, scaling as $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1+(T\epsilon)^{-1})$ with only polylogarithmic dependence on $h^{-1}$.

**Method.** The core technique involves using a multilevel estimator based on encoding the fine–coarse cancellation within a shifted Ritz–Schur factorization to avoid direct block encoding of high-resolution operators.

**Model / system.** The model is the heat equation ($\partial_t u + L u = 0$) solved via finite element discretization, leading to a semi-discrete linear ODE system $\dot{\mathbf{y}}_h = -L_h \mathbf{y}_h$. The analysis covers both direct semigroup estimation and multilevel correction.

**Key observables.** Linear and quadratic observables of the solution operator, such as regional average heat content or local mass flux ($\chi=0, 1, 2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Target time $T$, desired accuracy $\epsilon$, and mesh size $h$. The complexity is shown to be independent of readout order $\chi$ for low-order derivatives.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on specific access assumptions regarding the block encoding of shifted Ritz maps, and the analysis uses Galerkin approximation theory results for error bounding.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes; the structure is based on comparing complexity costs across different estimation methods (LMS vs. direct semigroup vs. corrected-resolvent).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem of mesh dependence in quantum PDE algorithms, then introduces and analyzes a multilevel estimator using shifted Ritz–Schur factorization to coherently place fine–coarse cancellation before measurement.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Can a quantum PDE algorithm avoid the polynomial cost of resolving a fine spatial mesh? For standard fixed-order discretizations, direct classical methods require work polynomial in $h^{-1}$, or equivalently in the number of spatial degrees of freedom $N_h=Θ(h^{-d})$. Direct quantum implementations of a parabolic semigroup still have coherent complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{T}/h)$, and gradient-dependent observables such as heat flux and dissipation introduce additional mesh dependence. Decay of the solution norm will further suppress the postselection probability for preparing a normalized final state.   We develop a multilevel quantum algorithm that estimates linear and quadratic observables $directly$ and places the fine--coarse cancellation inside the circuit before measurement. A contour-based LCU reconstructs each target-time correction from a coherent family of shifted resolvent differences. Rather than block encoding the fine and coarse inverses separately, we encode their difference through a shifted Ritz--Schur factorization, exposing its $\mathcal O(h_\ell^2)$ two-grid normalization. For Fourier hierarchies, the corresponding SELECT oracle consists of a quantum Fourier or sine transform, a spectral-band selector, and reversible diagonal arithmetic. We also give a non-Fourier realization based on energy-orthogonal dyadic midpoint details in one dimension, together with structured tensor-product extensions under fixed-rank coefficient and access assumptions.   For readouts with derivative order $0\leχ\le2$, optimized amplitude estimation removes $all$ polynomial dependence on the finest mesh size. Under the stated access assumptions, both linear and quadratic observables can be estimated with complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1+(Tε)^{-1})$, with only polylogarithmic dependence on $h^{-1}$.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces a novel, scalable characterization platform built using standard 65-nm CMOS technology to measure multiple physical properties (microwave, thermal, electrical) simultaneously. By integrating these functions onto a single chip, the authors overcome limitations in reproducibility and scalability inherent in current bespoke experimental setups. This breakthrough enables more accessible and standardized quantum materials research.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of standardized, foundry-compatible hardware platforms is crucial for advancing quantum science by removing significant engineering bottlenecks associated with custom cryogenic setups.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Current quantum materials characterization methods are limited by custom, non-scalable hardware setups that cannot easily integrate multiple measurement modalities.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated a scalable, foundry-manufacturable CMOS platform capable of integrating microwave, thermal, and electrical probes for multimodal quantum sensing.

**Method.** They repurposed a commercial 65-nm CMOS process to functionally partition the metal stack into distinct subsystems within a small footprint.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an integrated chip built on a standard CMOS foundry platform, featuring interdigitated electrodes (IDEs) for electrical sensing and patterned inductors for microwave excitation. This allows for heterogeneous integration of various quantum measurements.

**Key observables.** Magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$), ODMR contrast ($>20\%$), $	ext{S}$-parameters, capacitance-voltage ($	ext{C–V}$) response, and SEM image sharpness metrics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Operating temperatures down to $1.75 	ext{ K}$, microwave power levels of $4–9 	ext{ dBm}$, and a platform size limited to $1 	ext{ mm}^2$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach relies on repurposing existing commercial CMOS back-end-of-line capabilities, and magnetic measurements involve transferring samples onto the chip.

**Figures summary.** Figures show schematic architecture partitioning (Fig 1), detailed measurement results including $	ext{S}$-parameters, $	ext{C–V}$ curves, and temperature dependence of susceptibility (Fig 2); ODMR benchmarking compares CMOS vs. antenna setups (Fig 4).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the need for scalable multimodal characterization to presenting measurements across multiple domains: RF/Microwave ($	ext{S}$-params, ODMR), Electrical ($	ext{C–V}$ on IDEs), and Thermal (resistance vs. T), culminating in a demonstration of integrated functionality.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum materials experiments increasingly rely on microwave, electrical, thermal, optical, and structural probes, but these capabilities are typically assembled from custom hardware that limits reproducibility and scalability. Here we show that a commercial 65-nm CMOS process can be repurposed as a passive, foundry-manufacturable characterization platform by functionally partitioning its metal stack into microwave, thermal, and electrical subsystems within a 1 mm2 footprint. The integrated RF architecture enables cryogenic magnetic susceptibility measurements of Fe3GeTe2 heterostructures at 1.75 K without sample-specific fabrication. We further demonstrate NV-center optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) with >20% contrast at 4-9 dBm microwave power, reducing power requirements by 20-25 dB relative to conventional antenna-based approaches while maintaining sensitivities of 2-3 uT/sqrt(Hz). We additionally confirm compatibility with in-situ electron-beam imaging, showing no measurable degradation in image quality upon device operation. These results establish a scalable, foundry-manufacturable platform for multimodal quantum sensing and materials characterization.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores how manipulating doping or electric fields can tune the electronic state of $	ext{MnBi}_2	ext{Te}_4$ bilayers across topological and conventional anomalous Hall regimes. By combining DFT calculations with Monte Carlo simulations, the authors demonstrate a versatile framework for engineering magnetic and transport properties in these materials. This offers direct pathways toward reconfigurable quantum devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state magnetism/topology, the concept of tuning quantum transport via external fields (gating) and controlling magnetic order parameters is highly relevant to engineered quantum materials platforms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the systematic electronic, magnetic, and topological phase transitions within ultrathin magnetic topological insulator bilayers.

**Main result.** Electrostatic gating or surface doping can drive a crossover from an insulating topological state to a conventional anomalous Hall regime, allowing for tunable quantum device engineering.

**Method.** Calculations combine first-principles DFT methods with tight-binding models and classical Heisenberg Monte Carlo simulations.

**Model / system.** The system is the $	ext{MnBi}_2	ext{Te}_4$ magnetic topological insulator, analyzed in both bulk and bilayer limits, considering changes in interlayer coupling (AFM to FM).

**Key observables.** Anomalous Hall Conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$), Magnetic Ordering Temperature ($T_c$), Fermi Level position relative to the gap, and Interlayer Coupling type.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping concentration (hole/electron doping), dimensionality (bilayer limit), and magnetic coupling strength.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on symmetry considerations ($\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant, $T$, $S$) to classify topological phases and uses DFT for electronic structure calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate band structures confirming the topological insulator state, edge spectra showing quantization/suppression of $\sigma_{xy}$, and WCC plots diagnosing topological invariants in different coupling regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the bulk properties (AFM vs FM) to establish the baseline topology, then focuses on the bilayer limit, detailing how doping or gating induces a crossover between quantized topological states and high-conductivity anomalous Hall states.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the two-dimensional limit, the intrinsic magnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4 provides a compelling platform for exploring thickness-dependent quantum states and their evolution under external perturbations. Using first-principles calculations and classical Heisenberg Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that electrostatic gating and surface chemical functionalization can drive a systematic crossover from the topological to the conventional anomalous Hall regime. This transition is governed by the simultaneous shift of the Fermi level away from the topological gap and a reversal of interlayer coupling from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic order. Results reveal that hole doping drives the Fermi level into the valence bands, inducing an exceptionally high anomalous Hall conductivity of 1127 S/cm arising from Berry curvature hot spots. In contrast, surface chemical doping drives a topological state where intrinsic $σ_{xy}$ is reduced from $e^2/h$ to $\sim 0.86\ e^2/h$ by the spectral coexistance of chiral edge mode with metallic bulk states of the two-dimensional film. Furthermore, we show that both tuning routes significantly enhance in-plane exchange interactions, leading to a substantial increase in the magnetic ordering temperature relative to the pristine bilayer. These results establish a versatile framework for the simultaneous engineering of topological, magnetic, and transport properties in ultrathin MnBi2Te4, offering direct implications for the development of reconfigurable quantum devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically examines quantum teleportation fidelity when one participant accelerates relative to an inertial observer. It shows that while the Unruh effect predicts entanglement loss due to acceleration, a subsequent anti-Unruh effect causes the fidelity to recover and approach perfect transmission at high accelerations. This suggests relativistic motion can actively protect or enhance quantum information transfer.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses how fundamental spacetime effects (acceleration/Unruh effect) impact quantum communication protocols like teleportation, providing theoretical insights into relativistic quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how relativistic acceleration affects the fidelity of quantum teleportation, specifically contrasting the expected degradation from the Unruh effect with potential recovery mechanisms from the anti-Unruh effect.

**Main result.** The anti-Unruh effect can protect and enhance quantum correlations, causing the teleportation fidelity to increase monotonically towards unity at high accelerations. This demonstrates that acceleration can be an exploitable resource for maintaining quantum information.

**Method.** The analysis uses perturbative methods to calculate the reduced density matrix of the shared entanglement resource by tracing out the field modes interacting with Unruh-DeWitt detectors.

**Model / system.** The system models standard quantum teleportation where one participant (Rob) undergoes uniform acceleration in Minkowski spacetime, while Alice remains inertial. The interaction is mediated by a massive scalar field ($\phi$) coupled to an Unruh-DeWitt detector.

**Key observables.** Teleportation fidelity ($F$ or $A_F$), entanglement (Concurrence $C$), and information gain ($\Delta S$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Proper acceleration ($a$), detector energy gap ($\Omega$), field mass ($m$), and coupling constant ($\lambda$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on a first-order perturbative truncation of the evolution operator in the weak-coupling regime.

**Figures summary.** Figures show that for small energy gaps, fidelity increases monotonically with acceleration; for larger gaps, the crossover between Unruh degradation and anti-Unruh enhancement is visible in both concurrence and fidelity plots.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the relativistic setup using UDW detectors coupled to a scalar field. It then calculates entanglement measures (concurrence) and average teleportation fidelity by partial tracing over field modes, analyzing the dependence on acceleration $a$ and gap $\Omega$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate standard quantum teleportation in a relativistic setting where one participant, Rob, undergoes uniform acceleration while Alice remains inertial. Rob interacts locally with a massive scalar field modeled by an Unruh-DeWitt detector. We show that for small detector energy gaps, the entanglement shared between Alice and Rob increases monotonically with acceleration. For larger gaps, entanglement initially decreases at low accelerations due to the Unruh effect, but is subsequently restored and enhanced at higher accelerations as a consequence of the anti-Unruh effect. This behavior is associated with a reduction of the effective detector temperature, leading to a recovery of quantum coherence previously lost to the field. As a result, the teleportation fidelity increases with acceleration and approaches unity in the high-acceleration regime. Our results demonstrate that the anti-Unruh effect can protect and recover quantum information, providing a potential mechanism to mitigate relativistic degradation of quantum correlations.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces an efficient scheme to distribute GHZ-equivalent graph states across noisy quantum repeater networks. By combining state merging with Minimum Steiner Tree optimization, the authors achieve linear scaling in resources while explicitly minimizing decoherence accumulation during transmission. This provides a practical framework for realizing large-scale quantum communication protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly tackles practical limitations in quantum networking—namely decoherence and resource scaling—by providing a concrete, optimized protocol for distributing complex entangled states like graph states.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses the challenge of efficiently distributing GHZ-equivalent entangled states across large, repeater-based quantum networks while actively mitigating decoherence effects.

**Main result.** A novel scheme was proposed that achieves linear scaling in both qubit usage and controlled gate count ($O(N)$) for graph state distribution, proving its effectiveness via simulation.

**Method.** The approach combines a specialized state merging technique with an optimization framework modeled after the Minimum Steiner Tree problem to route entanglement efficiently.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a quantum network composed of repeaters connected by quantum channels. The target resource is graph states, which are LOCC-equivalent to GHZ states, used for protocols like QKD.

**Key observables.** End-to-end fidelity, qubit usage scaling ($O(N)$), controlled gate count scaling (linear), and total physical transmission length.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoherence rates, channel weights (physical lengths), and the number of nodes/edges in the network graph.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that decoherence during long-distance transmission is the limiting factor, necessitating repeaters; future work suggests incorporating heterogeneous noise models beyond simple physical length.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate examples of star and complete graph states, the process flow for state merging using auxiliary qubits and Y-basis measurements, and qubit distribution methods in repeater chains.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem by defining the need for efficient resource distribution. It details a novel scheme involving state merging (Section 3.1) followed by optimizing the network topology via an MST formulation (Section 3.2). The appendices provide mathematical proofs regarding gate equivalences and measurement calculations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

This study proposes a novel scheme for distributing GHZ-equivalent states across repeater-based quantum networks, with particular focus on the analysis and mitigation of decoherence effects during transmission. The proposed scheme enables remote users to share graph states, which can be leveraged to implement various quantum communication protocols, such as quantum key distribution and quantum secret sharing. Compared with existing approaches, the proposed distributed scheme requires only O(N) qubits without introducing redundant entanglement structures. Together with the linear-scaling merging procedure in both controlled gate count and qubit usage, the proposed framework supports more efficient large-scale graph state distribution. To evaluate its feasibility and correctness, this study utilizes the quantum network simulation tool, NetSquid, to implement the proposed scheme. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach is both effective and practical for executing quantum communication protocols within quantum networks.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work examines the limits of quantum work extraction reliability by comparing state-aware versus phase-independent protocols. It proves that while the average energy extracted (work rate) can be universal regardless of input knowledge, achieving optimal exponential reliability requires retaining precise knowledge of the system's initial state. The findings highlight a critical gap between these two measures of performance.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous mathematical tools (Remez inequality) to distinguish between average thermodynamic performance and finite-time operational robustness, which is crucial when designing quantum engines or communication protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the first-order universality observed in asymptotic quantum work extraction extends to reliability, which is characterized by the exponential decay rate of failure.

**Main result.** Input-state knowledge can be irrelevant for the average work rate but remains indispensable for achieving optimal exponential reliability bounds.

**Method.** The authors use finite-blocklength identities and apply a trigonometric Remez inequality to upgrade minimax optimization problems into pointwise theorems regarding error exponents.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on quantum work extraction from a coherent qubit time-translation orbit using a two-level work battery, comparing state-aware protocols against phase-independent ones.

**Key observables.** Asymptotic Work Rate ($D(ho\|	au)$), Reliability Exponents ($B_{	ext{aware}}^{	ext{GPO}}$, $B_{	ext{aware}}^{	ext{TO}}$), and Failure Probability ($\epsilon_n \sim e^{-nB}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The reliability parameter $r$, the coherence time $	heta \in [0, 2\pi)$, and the block length $n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing exact finite-blocklength identities between different extraction protocols and using large-deviation theory for asymptotic limits.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates finite reliability branches, comparing common (phase-independent) exponents to state-aware GPO exponents, showing separation windows.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing an exact identity between Gibbs-preserving extraction on an orbit and thermal operations. It then uses Remez's theorem to upgrade this minimax result to a pointwise statement, culminating in the comparison of state-aware vs. phase-independent reliability exponents for specific qubit families.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Universal work extraction shows that input-state knowledge is unnecessary to attain the asymptotic free-energy rate. We ask whether this first-order universality extends to reliability, the exponential decay rate of extraction failure. In the work-battery fidelity formulation, we prove that no phase-independent Gibbs-preserving protocol can retain the state-aware Gibbs-preserving exponent throughout a coherent qubit time-translation orbit: at every positive target rate, its worst pointwise exponent is bounded by the corresponding state-aware thermal-operation value. The proof first establishes an exact finite-blocklength identity between phase-robust Gibbs-preserving extraction and state-aware thermal extraction. A trigonometric Remez inequality then upgrades this minimax identity to a pointwise theorem by ruling out exponential localization of the worst phase. For an explicit coherent-qubit family, known-phase Gibbs-preserving extraction is error free, whereas every phase-independent protocol has a finite worst-pointwise exponent. Thus input-state knowledge can be irrelevant to the first-order work rate yet indispensable for optimal exponential reliability.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a detailed theory describing how local noise corrupts measurements used to characterize unknown quantum states. It derives an exponential scaling law for this noise bias based on the geometry (light cone) of the measured observable. The result proposes a practical calibration protocol that allows researchers to estimate properties of large observables by only measuring small, easily accessible strings.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides crucial theoretical tools for quantifying and mitigating hardware imperfections (noise) in quantum characterization protocols, directly impacting the feasibility of running complex algorithms on NISQ devices by linking error to operator dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses how local gate and readout errors bias the reconstruction of quantum observables obtained via randomized measurements (like classical shadows) on near-term hardware.

**Main result.** It establishes an exponential scaling law for noise damping ($\log \eta_k \propto -k$) related to the 'light cone' geometry of the measured Pauli operator, enabling a small-string calibration protocol.

**Method.** The authors develop a microscopic description using the Heisenberg picture and path averaging to derive an activated formula for the noisy Pauli coefficient, analyzed via cumulant expansion.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on locally scrambled shallow circuits in one dimension, modeling noise as weak local CPTP channels independent of random gates. The system is studied using randomized measurements applied to quantum states.

**Key observables.** Damping ratio ($\eta_k$) quantifying the noise bias for an operator $\hat{P}_k$, and the scaling parameters $\alpha$ and $eta$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Circuit depth ($d$), size of contiguous observable string ($k$), and the nature/strength of local Pauli noise (e.g., anisotropic, fluctuating).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes weak local CPTP noise independent of sampled random gates; linear scaling is assumed to hold for large $k$ away from boundaries.

**Figures summary.** Figures demonstrate the exponential decay ($\log \eta = -\alpha k - eta$) of the damping ratio for various circuits (Random Clifford, iSWAP) and show that small-string measurements can calibrate estimates for larger, complex observables.

**Paper structure.** The paper moves from developing a microscopic noise model based on activated path averaging to deriving the light-cone scaling law. It then verifies this scaling numerically using two-qubit circuits under various noise types, culminating in demonstrating a practical small-string calibration protocol.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Randomized measurements provide an efficient way to extract physical properties of an unknown quantum state from limited data. On near-term hardware, gate and readout errors bias the reconstructed observables. Here we develop a microscopic description of this bias for locally scrambled shallow circuits. Independent local twirling reduces local implementation noise to stochastic Pauli damping, and a noise event contributes only when it overlaps the Heisenberg evolution of the measured Pauli operator. This gives an activated path-average formula for the noisy Pauli coefficient. In one-dimensional shallow circuits, the activated noise volume grows linearly with the size of a contiguous observable, leading to an exponential damping ratio. We verify this scaling for two-qubit random Clifford and locally scrambled iSWAP circuits with two-qubit Pauli noise, including spatial fluctuations and temporal drift. The scaling supports a small-string calibration protocol that predicts larger string observables without learning the full noisy measurement channel. Our result relates the noise bias of shallow-shadow protocols directly to operator-evolving dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a mathematically rigorous, operator-centric framework for variational quantum eigensolvers applied to systems like the Ising chain. It introduces an exact algebraic pruning rule and critically analyzes adaptive operator selection under realistic finite-shot measurement constraints. The findings demonstrate that advanced selection policies, particularly 'racing,' are crucial for achieving high accuracy with minimal experimental resources.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical formulation connecting Pauli words to Clifford algebra and deriving an exact pruning rule is highly valuable for developing scalable quantum simulation tools that can handle the complexity of large circuits while remaining computationally tractable.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses developing an efficient, operator-centric framework for variational quantum algorithms (VQE) while overcoming the practical bottleneck of selecting relevant operators from limited finite measurements.

**Main result.** A systematic local odd-Y Pauli pool achieves extremely low relative energy errors ($<1.3 	imes 10^{-12}$) for small systems, and a 'racing' selection policy significantly improves measurement efficiency over fixed or uniform strategies in finite-shot tests.

**Method.** It utilizes the complex Clifford algebra to represent quantum operators sparsely, derives an exact gradient rule based on Pauli word structure (transpose-parity rule), and compares multiple adaptive operator selection policies under noisy, finite-shot measurements.

**Model / system.** The primary model tested is the open transverse-field Ising chain ($H = -\sum Z_j Z_{j+1} - h \sum X_j$) within the context of VQE. The formalism operates on $n$-qubit systems using Pauli words.

**Key observables.** Relative energy error ($\epsilon_E$), ADAPT selection gradient components ($G_P$), and success rates/median shot counts for different selection policies.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size ($n=4, 5, 6$), measurement budget (finite shots), and the confidence interval parameter $\kappa$ used in selection heuristics.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on an operator-centric algebraic formulation; finite-shot results are based on heuristic confidence bounds that do not guarantee coverage or account for full covariance.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare performance metrics (median $\epsilon E$, IQR) across different selection strategies (Fixed, Uniform, Racing) as the measurement ceiling increases, showing 'racing' maintains high success rates with fewer shots.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the algebraic framework using Clifford algebra and derives pruning rules. It then applies this to the TFIM Hamiltonian for VQE ansatzes. The core contribution involves comparing selection policies (Fixed vs. Uniform vs. Racing) under finite-shot measurement constraints, culminating in quantitative performance summaries.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a sparse operator-centric realization of $n$-qubit variational quantum algorithms in the complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(2n,\mathbb{C}) \cong M(2^n,\mathbb{C})$. Density operators, gates, observables, channels, fermionic modes, and adaptive-selection observables are represented in one Pauli-word algebra, with the Jordan--Wigner map providing the exact bridge to anticommuting Clifford generators. We distinguish general Pauli-word rotations from Spin-group rotors and derive an exact transpose-parity rule: for real Hamiltonians and real states, every candidate Pauli word containing an even number of $Y$ factors has zero ADAPT gradient, while odd-$Y$ rotations preserve the real sector. For the critical open transverse-field Ising chain, a depth-three Hamiltonian variational ansatz gives relative energy errors $4.84\times10^{-5}$, $2.19\times10^{-3}$, and $3.67\times10^{-3}$ for $n=4,5,6$. A compact local ADAPT pool is exact at $n=4$ but leaves residual errors at larger sizes; a systematic contiguous three-local odd-$Y$ pool reaches relative errors below $1.3\times10^{-12}$ for $n\leq6$. In 100-seed finite-shot tests at $n=4$, fixed-shot selection succeeds in $0/100$ runs, whereas uniform escalation and confidence-bound racing each succeed in $84/100$ runs; racing lowers median shots by $34\%$. We claim no asymptotic speedup over matrix methods. The contribution is a corrected algebraic formulation, an exact pool-pruning rule, and a reproducible study of measurement-limited adaptive selection.

</details>
